name: Mohammad Javadi Balakan
meta_description: Mohammad Javadi (MJ) Balakan is an experimental physicist who builds superconducting quantum devices. Research on topological superconductivity in Fe(Te,Se), 2D materials and silicon optoelectronics.
lead: I build and measure superconducting quantum devices. My research looks for topological superconductivity, a route to fault-tolerant qubits, in nanoscale rings of the iron-based superconductor Fe(Te,Se).
now: Research Scientist at a stealth-mode startup in the Bay Area. Previously Research Scientist and Postdoctoral Fellow at SUNY Albany's College of Nanotechnology, Science, and Engineering, and Postdoctoral Associate at the University of Tehran.
research_intro: For more than a decade I have taken devices from idea to measurement: design, cleanroom fabrication, and low-noise electrical characterization from room temperature down to a few kelvin.

themes.title: Topological superconductivity for quantum computing
themes.text: Topological superconductors can host Majorana modes, the building block of qubits that resist errors by design. I fabricate hBN-encapsulated Fe(Te,Se) rings a few hundred nanometres across and measure them at cryogenic temperatures with low-noise electronics. These devices show half-quantum flux oscillations, coherent edge transport, and a built-in magnetization of the superconducting condensate.

themes.title: 2D materials for CMOS-compatible devices
themes.text: Combining atom-thin materials with silicon could give chips new functions at lower energy. I measured how charge crosses the graphene–silicon interface, calculated the efficiency limit of graphene solar cells, and grew borophene, a 2D metal for ultrathin interconnects, by chemical vapor deposition for the first time.

themes.title: Hybrid organic–silicon optoelectronics
themes.text: Coating silicon with a conductive polymer gives light sensors that are made at low temperature and can run without external power. I worked out how charge moves through these junctions, then built large-area position-sensitive detectors and self-powered photodiodes with a photovoltage responsivity of 10⁶ V/W.

themes.title: Solar cells, nanostructures and transport modeling
themes.text: My early work paired nanostructured solar cells and detectors with computer models of how electrons diffuse through disordered materials. Micro-patterning porous TiO₂ guided electrons toward the electrode and made their diffusion length about three times longer.
